title: Gel electrophoresis
wiki_lead:
Gel electrophoresis is a method for separation and analysis of biomacromolecules (DNA, RNA, proteins, etc.) and their fragments, based on their size and charge as they move through a gel under an electric field. It is used in clinical chemistry to separate proteins by charge or size and in biochemistry and molecular biology to separate a mixed population of DNA and RNA fragments by length, to estimate the size of DNA and RNA fragments, or to separate proteins by charge.
Nucleic acid molecules are separated by applying an electric field to move the negatively charged molecules through a gel matrix of agarose, polyacrylamide, or other substances. Shorter molecules move faster and migrate farther than longer ones because shorter molecules flow more easily through the pores of the gel. This phenomenon is called sieving. Proteins are separated by the charge in agarose because the pores of the gel are too large to sieve proteins. Gel electrophoresis can also be used for the separation of nanoparticles.
Gel electrophoresis uses a gel as an anticonvective medium or sieving medium during electrophoresis. Gels suppress the thermal convection caused by the application of the electric field  and can also serve to maintain the finished separation so that a post-electrophoresis stain can be applied. DNA gel electrophoresis is usually performed for analytical purposes, often after amplification of DNA via polymerase chain reaction (PCR), but may be used as a preparative technique for other methods such as mass spectrometry, RFLP, PCR, cloning, DNA sequencing, or Southern blotting for further characterization.

Physical basis

Electrophoresis is a process that enables the sorting of molecules based on charge, size, or shape. Using an electric field, molecules such as DNA can be made to move through a gel made of agarose or polyacrylamide. The electric field consists of a negative charge at one end which pushes the molecules through the gel and a positive charge at the other end that pulls the molecules through the gel. The molecules being sorted are dispensed into a well in the gel material. The gel is placed in an electrophoresis chamber, which is then connected to a power source. When the electric field is applied, the larger molecules move more slowly through the gel while the smaller molecules move faster. The different sized molecules form distinct bands on the gel.
The term "gel" in this instance refers to the matrix used to contain, then separate the target molecules. In most cases, the gel is a crosslinked polymer whose composition and porosity are chosen based on the specific weight and composition of the target to be analyzed. When separating proteins or small nucleic acids (DNA, RNA, or oligonucleotides), the gel is usually composed of different concentrations of acrylamide and a cross-linker, producing different sized mesh networks of polyacrylamide. When separating larger nucleic acids (greater than a few hundred bases), the preferred matrix is purified agarose. In both cases, the gel forms a solid yet porous matrix. Acrylamide, in contrast to polyacrylamide, is a neurotoxin and must be handled using appropriate safety precautions to avoid poisoning. Agarose is composed of long unbranched chains of uncharged carbohydrates without cross-links, resulting in a gel with large pores allowing for the separation of macromolecules and macromolecular complexes.
Electrophoresis refers to the electromotive force (EMF) that is used to move the molecules through the gel matrix. By placing the molecules in wells in the gel and applying an electric field, the molecules will move through the matrix at different rates, determined largely by their mass when the charge-to-mass ratio (Z) of all species is uniform. grok_lead: Gel electrophoresis is a laboratory technique used to separate charged biomolecules, such as DNA, RNA, and proteins, based on their size and electrical charge by applying an electric current through a porous gel matrix. In this process, the gel acts as a molecular sieve, allowing smaller molecules to migrate faster toward the positive electrode (anode) while larger ones move more slowly, enabling the resolution of fragments based on relatively small size differences. The technique, which emerged in the mid-20th century with advancements in gel media like starch and polyacrylamide in the 1950s and 1960s, has become a cornerstone of molecular biology for its simplicity, versatility, and ability to handle diverse sample types. The principle relies on the differential mobility of charged particles in an electric field, where negatively charged nucleic acids move through the gel's pores under the influence of electrophoresis buffer, typically containing ions to conduct the current. Common gel types include agarose, derived from seaweed polysaccharides, which is ideal for separating larger DNA fragments (100 base pairs to 25 kilobases) due to its larger pore size, and polyacrylamide, which offers finer resolution for smaller DNA pieces, RNA, or proteins through its denser matrix. Polyacrylamide gels, often used in denaturing conditions with sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) for proteins, linearize molecules to separate primarily by mass, as seen in SDS-PAGE protocols. Gel electrophoresis finds broad applications in research, diagnostics, and forensics, including DNA fragment analysis for genetic mapping, protein purity assessment in biochemistry, and identification of genetic disorders through techniques like hemoglobin electrophoresis. It underpins methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) product verification, restriction enzyme digests, and even forensic DNA profiling by enabling the visualization of separated bands via stains like ethidium bromide under UV light. Ongoing refinements, such as pulsed-field gel electrophoresis for very large DNA molecules, continue to expand its utility in genomics and proteomics.
